heroDescription: From the AFL's opening game to Orange Crush, John Elway's comebacks and championship defenses, explore the people and moments behind Broncos Country.
timelineKicker: From AFL beginnings to three Super Bowl titles

timeline.title: Denver joins the new AFL
timeline.description: Bob Howsam received an AFL charter franchise on August 14, 1959. The Broncos would begin playing the following year.

timeline.title: The AFL's first game belongs to Denver
timeline.description: On September 9, Denver beat the Boston Patriots 13–10 in the AFL's first regular-season game, opening the franchise's inaugural season with a win.

timeline.title: Orange and blue arrive
timeline.description: Under coach and general manager Jack Faulkner, Denver replaced its original brown-and-gold look. The orange uniforms debuted in a September 7 win over San Diego.

timeline.title: A first trip to the Super Bowl
timeline.description: A 12–2 regular season and the Orange Crush defense set up Denver's breakthrough. The Broncos beat Oakland 20–17 in the AFC Championship on January 1, 1978, to reach Super Bowl XII.

timeline.title: John Elway comes to Denver
timeline.description: On May 2, the Broncos acquired John Elway from the Baltimore Colts. The trade brought Denver the quarterback who would lead its offense for sixteen seasons.

timeline.title: The Drive
timeline.description: The 1986 season's AFC Championship was played on January 11, 1987. Elway led a 98-yard touchdown march to tie Cleveland before Denver won 23–20 in overtime.

timeline.title: Denver wins its first Lombardi Trophy
timeline.description: The 1997 season ended with a 31–24 victory over Green Bay in Super Bowl XXXII on January 25, 1998. MVP Terrell Davis ran for 157 yards and three touchdowns.

timeline.title: Back-to-back champions
timeline.description: Denver repeated after the 1998 season, defeating Atlanta in Super Bowl XXXIII on January 31, 1999. Elway earned the game's MVP award in his final NFL appearance.

timeline.title: A new stadium carries the Mile High name
timeline.description: The Broncos opened their new regular-season home, then called Invesco Field at Mile High, with a 31–20 victory over the Giants on September 10.

timeline.title: Peyton Manning starts a new chapter
timeline.description: Manning joined Denver and earned Comeback Player of the Year after missing the previous season through injury. His four Broncos seasons produced four AFC West titles.

timeline.title: An offense rewrites the record book
timeline.description: Manning threw 55 touchdown passes as Denver scored 606 regular-season points. Both totals set NFL records, and Manning earned his fifth league MVP award.

timeline.title: Defense delivers Super Bowl 50
timeline.description: Denver capped the 2015 season by beating Carolina 24–10 on February 7, 2016. Super Bowl MVP Von Miller recorded 2.5 sacks and forced two fumbles in Manning's final game.

eras.title: AFL roots
eras.description: Denver began as an AFL charter member. The early years brought the league's first regular-season win, a growing local following and the foundations of a permanent football home in Colorado.

eras.title: Orange Crush and Mile High
eras.description: The Orange Crush name grew from Denver's late-1970s defense. In the stands, the South Stands and the stomping tradition known as Mile High Thunder became part of Broncos Country's identity.

eras.title: The championship breakthrough
eras.description: Mike Shanahan became head coach in 1995 and led Denver to consecutive Super Bowl wins after the 1997 and 1998 seasons. His teams made the running game a central part of their success.

eras.title: Manning and the No Fly Zone
eras.description: The 2015 champions paired Manning's experience with Von Miller, DeMarcus Ware and the No Fly Zone secondary. A defense featuring Aqib Talib and Chris Harris Jr. helped secure Denver's third title.

methodology: This independent overview draws on Denver Broncos historical records and the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Timeline years follow the football season where relevant; descriptions give the calendar dates of postseason games. Player selections illustrate different eras and are not a ranking. Each timeline entry, era and number links to its source.
